You can't divide by zero, but you can (in some cases) assign a value to a function at 0. Following the example of the video, say you are working on the Reals and say you have f(x)=1/x. Here you can't divide by 0, as there is no limit (value) you can assign to f(0) that is consistent for all cases (coming from the right and from the left, as per the video example). On the other hand, if you have f(x)=sin(x)/x you can assign a value to f(0) that is consistent with all cases, in this case the limit from the right and from the left is equal to 1, so we can replace the undefined sin(0)/0 by 1.

If you go to multiple variables you face the problem that you have now infinite ways to approach 0 (as opposed to 2 in the real line), but some tricks can still be done. A very common one in 2D (either complex numbers or (x,y) coordinates) is to express quantities in polar coordinates, if you can show that the value of f(r,theta) is independent of theta when r->0, then you can replace the value of f(0,theta) by the limit, since the direction of approach does not matter (this is similar to the second example when they talked about f(x,y)=x/y, which in polar coordinates becomes f(r,theta)=(rcos(theta))/(rsin(theta))=cot(theta), which is dependent on theta and therefore has no limit at f(0,theta)).
